```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
moisture <- c(6, 10, 13, 22, 26, 30)
height <- c(8, 13, 10, 18, 15, 21)
new_moisture <- 16
new_height <- 14

fit_line <- lm(height ~ moisture)
fit_curve <- splinefun(moisture, height, method = "natural")
pred_line <- unname(predict(fit_line, data.frame(moisture = new_moisture)))
pred_curve <- fit_curve(new_moisture)
rss_line <- sum(resid(fit_line)^2)
f1 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

**NRES 746, Week 10, Lecture 1: Connect the Dots**

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

**Instructions:** Work alone on Part 1 (about 3 minutes), then compare
with a neighbor for Part 2. Keep laptops closed.

## The data

Seedling height after one growing season in six restoration plots that
differ in soil moisture.

```{r dots, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.3}
par(mar = c(3.2, 3.6, 0.5, 0.5), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 35), ylim = c(0, 25), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Soil moisture (%)", ylab = "Seedling height (cm)")
abline(v = seq(0, 35, 1), h = seq(0, 25, 1), col = "grey93")
abline(v = seq(0, 35, 5), h = seq(0, 25, 5), col = "grey80")
abline(v = new_moisture, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
text(new_moisture, 24, "new plot", pos = 4, cex = 0.85, col = "grey30")
abline(fit_line, col = ans_col, lwd = 2)
xs <- seq(4, 32, 0.1)
lines(xs, pmin(fit_curve(xs), 25), col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
points(moisture, height, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
points(new_moisture, new_height, pch = 4, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2.5, col = ans_col)
legend("bottomright", c("straight line (least squares)", "curve through every point",
                        "the new plot, measured later"),
       col = ans_col, lwd = c(2, 2, 2.5), lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 4),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85, text.col = ans_col)
box()
```

## Part 1: Two models (individual)

**1a.** On the figure, draw (i) a straight line that fits the six points
well, and (ii) a smooth curve that passes through every point.

\ansbegin

One example of each is drawn above; yours will differ somewhat.

\ansend

**1b.** Which of your two models has the smaller sum of squared
residuals for these six plots? \ans{The curve: its residuals are all 0
(the least-squares line's sum is `r f1(rss_line)`).}

**1c.** A seventh plot has 16% soil moisture (dashed line). Read off each
model's predicted height. Straight line: \ans{about `r f1(pred_line)`}
cm. Curve: \ans{about `r f1(pred_curve)` (for the curve above)} cm.
Which prediction would you bet on, and why?

\ansbegin

The line. The curve's dip between 13% and 22% comes from one low plot
(13%), which is more likely noise than a real effect of moisture. The
new plot measured `r new_height` cm.

\ansend

## Part 2: Compare (with a neighbor)

**2a.** Lay your figures side by side. Which agree more closely between
the two of you, your straight lines or your curves? What does that tell
you about judging a model only by how well it fits the data used to
fit it?

\ansbegin

The straight lines agree closely. The curves match at the six points
but wander differently between them. A curve through every point
always fits perfectly, so fit to the same data can't tell a good model
from an overfit one; we need a penalty for complexity or new data to
test against.

\ansend
